ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic медвѣдь (medvědĭ), from Proto-Slavic *medvědь. Literally, “one that eats mead/honey”. Compare Russian медое́д (medojéd), composed of the same roots. Also compare Sanskrit मध्वद् (madhvad, “honey- or mead-eating”). Compare typologically Bulgarian лакомец (lakomec, “wolverine”), Macedonian лакомец (lakomec, “glutton, wolverine”).

ety.text: раст- (rast-) + -е́ние (-énije). Compare typologically о́вощ (óvošč) (<<~ Proto-Indo-European *h₂weg-, whence also Lithuanian augti, whence augalas); были́нка (bylínka), быльё (bylʹjó) (akin to прибы́ть (pribýtʹ), прибыва́ть (pribyvátʹ)), Ancient Greek φυτόν (phutón) << φύω (phúō). Also compare English grass (akin to grow; both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁-, whence also Latin herba, grāmen); Mongolian ургамал (urgamal) (< ургах (urgax, “to grow”)).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarovъ, from *jaro (“spring”). Constructed as if from *яр (*jar) + -ово́й (-ovój); compare dialectal яр (jar, “heat, fire”), Old East Slavic ꙗра (jara, “spring”). First attested in the 14th century.
